This section explains the structure of the ACC value chain and the distribution of value across its stages. Data shows that materials and components account for more than 70% of a lithium-ion cell’s total value, with anode and cathode active materials, electrolytes, and separators contributing about 50%, and the remaining 23% arising from current collectors, binders, packaging, manufacturing overheads, etc. The results also highlight India’s progress in midstream manufacturing. Announced domestic capacities for 2025–2030 include 300,000 tonnes per annum (TPA) of anode material, 250,000 TPA of Lithium Ferro Phosphate (LFP) cathode, 70,000 TPA of Nickel Manganese Cobalt (NMC) cathode, 12,000 TPA of electrolyte, and 40,000 TPA of aluminum foil, reflecting movement from planning to pilot and early commercial stages. In addition, cell-manufacturing capacity is expanding rapidly. Under the ACC PLI scheme, 40 GWh has already been awarded, and the broader industry pipeline PLI and non-PLI combined is projected to reach about 142 GWh by 2030, with approximately 85 GWh expected to be operational by then. These results show the scale at which India must build its supply chain to meet rising ACC demand, projected to grow from 17–20 GWh in 2025 to 100–197 GWh in 2030, and underline the need for strong domestic capability in both component production and cell manufacturing.

The ACC battery (essentially a lithium-ion battery) (in the current scenario, in India, the term advanced chemistry cell primarily refers to lithium-ion batteries, as other chemistries are still at early R&D or pilot stages) value chain consists of three key stages: Upstream, Midstream, and Downstream (Figure 1). The Upstream phase involves the extraction and refining of raw materials, as well as the sourcing of essential elements such as lithium, cobalt, and nickel. The Midstream phase focuses on manufacturing battery components, including cathodes, anodes, electrolytes, and separators, which are then assembled into battery cells. Finally, the Downstream stage integrates these cells into battery packs for EVs and energy storage applications, followed by end-of-life recycling to recover valuable materials and promote sustainability [19, 20].

Figure 2 presents an integrative framework linking policy drivers and demand signals to the upstream, midstream, and downstream segments of India’s battery value chain. It also maps key bottlenecks to the corresponding policy interventions discussed in the paper, thereby providing the holistic, value-chain-wide context.

The total value added from material processing, battery materials, and component manufacturing in the battery value chain is >70% in a cell [21], in which anode and cathode active materials, electrolytes, and separators alone account for approximately 50% [7] (Figure 3). This highlights the crucial role of localized material processing and component manufacturing in strengthening India’s ACC ecosystem. The 23% cost contribution from the ‘Others’ category reflects costs from packaging and encapsulation, inactive materials like adhesives, spacers, gaskets, thermal and safety components, basic electronics, and sensors, as well as manufacturing overheads such as utilities, cleanroom maintenance, and indirect consumables.

The ACC component manufacturing industry is evolving rapidly to meet the increasing demand from PLI and non-PLI companies. This supports India’s goal of reducing dependence on imports and creating a self-reliant battery supply chain. Figure 4 illustrates the key components being developed by Indian players across different stages of production. Currently, the manufacturing of these components is at various stages of development in India (planning, pilot scale, commercial scale). As the manufacturing ecosystem advances, the industry aims to achieve large-scale manufacturing capacities by 2025 and 2030, thereby catering to the growing demand for ACCs. With continued technological advancements, policy incentives, and private sector investments, the industry is set to achieve large-scale manufacturing capacities by 2025 and 2030 to cater to the growing demand for ACC batteries in EVs, stationary storage, and other applications [7].

Several factors influence the growth of ACCs, including policy initiatives to increase EV deployment, central policies that promote ACC and EV component manufacturing, state policy incentives for ACC manufacturing, and initiatives to secure the supply chain of critical materials. The Faster adoption and manufacturing of Hybrid and Electric Vehicles (FAME) India scheme, launched in 2015 to promote electric and hybrid vehicles, has been implemented in two phases with a focus on adoption incentives and charging infrastructure [22–25]. The PLI scheme aims to boost domestic manufacturing of ACC with a target battery capacity of 50 GWh, supported by a budget allocation of USD 20.6 Billion [3]. The scheme is designed to enhance domestic value addition, starting at 25% in the initial two years and increasing to 60% over five years, with incentive disbursements spread over this period. Capacity allocation ranges from 5 GWh to 20 GWh, ensuring flexibility for manufacturers. In January 2022, ten companies submitted bids for the program. By March 2022, the MHI selected four firms—Rajesh Exports Limited, Hyundai Global Motors Company Limited, Ola Electric Mobility Private Limited, and Reliance New Energy Limited—to participate in the scheme [4]. Subsequently, on 28 July 2022, Reliance New Energy Ltd., Ola Electric Mobility Pvt Ltd., and Rajesh Exports Ltd. signed agreements under the PLI scheme, initiating the construction of ACC battery Gigafactories in India. This marked a significant step toward strengthening the country’s energy storage and battery manufacturing ecosystem [4]. PLIs have also become effective for automotive products that indirectly support battery manufacturing. In September 2021, the Indian government approved a PLI scheme with an outlay of USD 29.5 Billion to strengthen the country’s manufacturing capacity for advanced automotive products [3]. The scheme aims to provide financial incentives to stimulate domestic manufacturing of advanced automotive technology products and encourage investments in the automotive manufacturing value chain. The implementation timeline for the scheme is 2022–23 to 2026–27. The National Critical Minerals Mission (NCMM) to secure reliable, cost-stable, and sustainable access to critical minerals essential for ACC manufacturing and clean energy technologies [26], The Champion OEM Incentive Scheme and Champion Component Incentive Scheme [3], the Mission for Advancement in High-Impact Areas (MAHA)—EV, launched under the Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF) [27], and other incentives offered by the GoI are designed to provide impetus to ACC manufacturing ecosystem in the country [28–32].

As of December 2023 [33], these incentives include capital subsidies, road tax exemptions, EV/ACC manufacturing subsidies, charging infrastructure subsidies, R&D support, battery recycling, and scrapping incentives, among others. Currently, the two most well-developed technologies in ACC batteries are (LFP) and NMC. However, as the battery industry continues to evolve, other promising chemistries, such as sodium-ion, lithium manganese iron phosphate (LMFP), and solid-state batteries, are gradually gaining attention for specialized applications [2]. Globally, and in India, based on industry inputs, the trend is expected to be dominated by the LFP technology by 2030 [35] due to its cost-effectiveness, safety, and thermal stability [34]. Although NMC chemistry is more energy-dense and offers a higher range per charge, its adoption is primarily concentrated in premium and high-performance EVs. The rise of battery-swapping infrastructure, especially in e3W and commercial fleets, further supports the widespread adoption of LFP batteries, as they offer stable performance and longer lifespans at a lower cost [7]. By 2030, the market will likely see a diversified mix of battery technologies, with LFP continuing to dominate mass-market applications (approximately 70%), NMC remaining relevant for high-performance and premium EVs (approximately 25%), and other emerging chemistries (approximately 5%) catering to specific use cases. Secondary data on chemistry adoption were supported by insights from consultations with OEMs, cell manufacturers, and component/material suppliers, who helped validate the factors influencing the shift across chemistries. Figure 7 provides a chemistry-wise split for ACC and captures projected share of various battery chemistries by 2030 [7]. This shift in battery technology trends will play a crucial role in shaping India’s EV adoption strategy, ensuring cost efficiency, energy security, and sustainability in the long run.

The Indian ACC battery manufacturing industry is gearing up significantly to cater to the domestic and global demand for ACC batteries. The GoI national program, in conjunction with the ACC PLI program, is a good starting point for developing the domestic battery manufacturing ecosystem. With the recent progress in the ACC PLI program, three companies have signed the PLI agreement for a capacity of 40 GWh and are all set to build their plants. The GoI is on the verge of closing the remaining capacity, marking a promising future for indigenous manufacturing. In addition to the capacity allocated under the ACC PLI scheme, more than ten companies have announced plans to build ACC gigafactories in India [35]. The IESA estimates that cumulative ACC manufacturing capacity will reach 142 GWh by 2030, with an estimated 85 GWh expected to be operational by then. Figure 8 provides the year-wise installation and operational estimates, highlighting the ramp-up from 1 GWh in 2024 to 142 GWh by 2030.

The PLI scheme remains a key driver, contributing 50 GWh by 2030, while the remaining capacity will come from non-PLI players such as Amara Raja, Exide, Lucas TVS, and other private investments. This diversified capacity growth underscores the industry’s momentum beyond government-backed programs, with non-PLI participants playing an equally critical role. It is important to note that gigafactories require time to stabilize operations and achieve full production efficiency. Based on conservative utilization factors (starting from approximately 30% in 2026 and rising to approximately 60% by 2030), effective operational capacity is projected to increase gradually from 9 GWh in 2027 to 85 GWh by 2030. These estimates are based on publicly announced gigafactory plans, while commissioning timelines, expected ramp-up, and operational feasibility were validated through stakeholder interviews and industry consultations. The capacity utilization rate has been assumed based on the discussions with industry stakeholders and considering the current developments of ACC gigafactories [36, 37]. This reflects a realistic ramp-up phase as new plants transition from commissioning to steady-state operations [7].

India’s ACC gigafactory development is currently underway, and until domestic production scales up, a significant portion of the demand will continue to be met through imported cells. Figure 9 illustrates the gap between India’s ACC supply and demand, highlighting the reliance on imports to bridge the shortfall in battery production.

In an ACC, raw materials account for the majority of the cost structure, comprising over 60% of total manufacturing costs. For instance, in an LFP cell, the cathode alone contributes approximately 30%, followed by the anode (approximately 15%), electrolyte (approximately 10%), and separator (approximately 7%). The balance is spread across current collectors, binders, additives, and assembly overheads. This emphasizes the urgent need to localize and incentivize component manufacturing—cathodes, anodes, separators, and electrolytes—under India’s ACC PLI and complementary schemes. By doing so, India can enhance domestic value addition, reduce reliance on imports, and build a resilient supply chain for its growing battery ecosystem. By 2025, India’s ACC demand is projected to reach approximately 17 GWh, while domestic production capacity will remain limited at approximately 2 GWh (based on the current developments, the ACC capacity by end of 2025 is estimated to be 2 GWh). Though the domestic capacity pipeline is projected to reach approximately 17 GWh by 2025, the sharp decline in global cell prices has delayed investments and slowed commissioning by domestic players. As a result, nearly 90% of the demand will be met through imports, primarily from China and other established battery-producing nations. Imports are expected to remain dominant in the initial years, accounting for approximately 87% in 2026 and approximately 76% in 2027.

A major shift is expected from 2028 onward, when new gigafactories commissioned under the PLI scheme and by private players begin scaling operations. As shown in the figure, India’s reliance on imports is projected to decline to 57% in 2028, fall sharply to 36% in 2029, and further reduce to just 15% by 2030. By then, domestic supply is estimated at approximately 85 GWh, compared to demand of approximately 100 GWh, indicating that India could meet the bulk of its requirements domestically by the end of the decade. This transition highlights the critical role of accelerated gigafactory expansion, localization of the midstream supply chain (anodes, cathodes, electrolytes, and separators), and sustained policy support in reducing dependence on imports. Even with strong growth, India will continue to import a portion of advanced cells and materials, but the trend indicates a substantial improvement in self-sufficiency compared to the current scenario. Ensuring raw material security, building refining and processing capacity, and scaling component manufacturing will remain central to achieving long-term sustainability in India’s ACC ecosystem.

The ACC PLI scheme has played a crucial role in establishing and supporting the growth of India’s local ACC component industry. With its mandate for minimum domestic value addition, the scheme has encouraged significant private sector investments across the upstream supply chain, particularly in anode, cathode, electrolyte, separator, and other essential components. In response, India has made substantial progress in establishing local manufacturing capabilities, which are currently at various stages of development, ranging from planning and pilot-scale operations to commercial and giga-scale manufacturing. More than 15 companies have already initiated the development of gigafactories for ACC component production, while several others are preparing to scale up or expand existing operations. Table 5 shows the manufacturers involved in producing different components [60, 61]. Based on the interviews of 20 industry experts deploying a questionnaire (the details of the industry experts and the questionnaire are provided in the supplementary materials), it is found that the major challenges hindering India’s ACC manufacturing ecosystem include dependence on raw materials from other countries, high capital costs, and policy gaps. However, there are emerging opportunities (the recommendations are based on the insights from stakeholder consultations and policy discussions) driven by government incentives, technological advancements, and growing EV demand.

The challenges highlighted in this paper are grounded in extensive stakeholder consultations conducted across multiple forums in 2024–25 (see Table S1). Primary challenges in domestic manufacturing are in terms of lack of availability of raw material, manufacturing facilities, skilled workforce, policy framework, policy innovation, global regulations, etc.

The most pressing challenge that India faces is the lack of access to several critical raw materials essential for ACC production. The country is 100% dependent on imports of high-purity lithium, cobalt, nickel, electrolyte precursors, and separator materials [62]. This over-reliance in terms of both cathode and anode material exposes the industry to global supply chain disruptions, price fluctuations, and geopolitical risks. The cathode materials, comprising lithium, nickel, cobalt, and manganese, and lithium iron phosphate has their distinct supply chain challenges [63]. For NMC batteries, India is entirely dependent on imports of Nickel Sulfate, Cobalt Sulfate, and Lithium Carbonate, sourcing these critical materials from China, Australia, and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) [19, 64, 65]. A significant challenge is India’s limited cobalt refining capabilities, making it difficult for India to secure a stable supply at competitive prices [60, 66]. Anodes, another crucial component of ACCs, are primarily made from graphite, which exists in natural and synthetic graphite. While India possesses about 8% of the world’s graphite reserves, it does not produce battery-grade natural graphite due to mining restrictions and environmental regulations. As a result, domestic manufacturers rely on imports [67, 68]. India has some domestic production capacity for synthetic graphite, primarily derived from coal tar pitch; however, the rapidly growing demand for ACCs may soon outpace local supply. To bridge this gap, the industry may need to import petroleum coke—a precursor material for synthetic graphite—from countries like the USA and the EU, further increasing reliance on foreign suppliers [35, 69–71].

India’s manufacturing capabilities for upstream and intermediate battery components are currently at various stages of development, ranging from planning to commercial production. While several companies have announced significant investments in the sector, the actual on-ground implementation remains slow due to funding challenges and the high capital costs associated with setting up gigafactories. Some firms have initiated pilot-scale production, but their ability to scale operations is hindered by the unavailability of key raw materials, forcing them to rely on imports of these materials. A few companies have achieved commercial-scale production, yet they remain highly dependent on foreign suppliers for critical battery components, which increases manufacturing costs and reduces their competitiveness in the global market. One of the biggest hurdles in battery manufacturing is the fragmented supply chain. The absence of a fully integrated domestic supply network forces manufacturers to source materials and components from multiple international suppliers, resulting in longer lead times, logistical inefficiencies, and increased costs [72]. Additionally, the high operating costs associated with battery production, particularly the need for stable and affordable electricity, pose another challenge. India’s industrial electricity tariffs are relatively high compared to China, where government subsidies help lower power costs for manufacturers [54].

Battery manufacturing is a highly technical and precision-driven process that requires expertise in electrochemistry, materials science, precision engineering, and automation. Unlike conventional manufacturing, it involves specialized machinery, complex chemical formulations, and strict quality control, necessitating a highly trained workforce to ensure efficiency and reliability. India lacks a well-established talent pool with expertise in electrode preparation, electrolyte formulation, cell assembly, battery management system (BMS) integration, and quality testing. In contrast, China, South Korea, Japan, and the European Union have developed their lithium-ion battery industries for decades, supported by strong academic and industrial training programs. These countries have built a competitive advantage by cultivating a workforce skilled in advanced battery technology. Bridging this skills gap through targeted training programs, industry collaborations, and academic partnerships will be critical to accelerating India’s ACC manufacturing capabilities [73].

Currently, there is no dedicated policy support or incentive program specifically promoting investments in ACC component manufacturing. While the ACC PLI scheme supports large-scale battery cell manufacturing, it does not directly benefit the processing of raw materials and the manufacture of components. This policy gap leaves domestic players struggling with funding constraints, infrastructure challenges, and regulatory hurdles, making it difficult to scale up production and achieve cost competitiveness with global suppliers. The key policy and regulatory challenges faced by ACC players include high capital investment in technology, complex and time-intensive environmental clearance, lack of access to technology and specialized raw materials, limited access to bank loans and financing, high R&D requirements, issues related to land acquisition, tariff complexity and customs bottlenecks, etc.

Global regulatory changes are becoming a key factor in determining the competitiveness of India’s ACC industry. The U.S. Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) restricts subsidies and tax credits to batteries manufactured domestically or sourced from FTA partners, effectively excluding Indian manufacturers due to the absence of an India–U.S. FTA. In addition, under the U.S. Reciprocal Tariff Regime, Indian battery and component exports face tariffs of around 25% (ongoing discussion), significantly reducing competitiveness in one of the world’s fastest-growing battery markets [74, 75]. The European Union’s Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA) sets supply diversification mandates, requiring member states to source at least 40% of their battery materials from EU or trusted partners, a threshold India cannot presently meet [76]. Meanwhile, China has imposed export restrictions on key materials such as graphite, gallium, and germanium, while controlling over 65% of global graphite processing and nearly 70% of LFP cathode capacity, leaving Indian manufacturers exposed to potential supply shortages and price shocks [77]. These restrictions collectively constrain India’s ability to access global incentives, raise the landed cost of raw materials, and intensify import dependence, underscoring the urgent need for India to accelerate trade agreements, expand domestic refining, and develop alternate material supply chains.

A central area of opportunity lies in securing reliable access to critical minerals through targeted bilateral trade agreements with countries such as the United States, Australia, and Chile. This would provide Indian firms with preferential access to supply chains for lithium, nickel, and cobalt, thereby reducing their vulnerability to price volatility and geopolitical risk. Expanding the scope of the PLI scheme to cover ACC component manufacturers would further stimulate investments in refining, recycling, and midstream processing. Establishing a dedicated Critical Raw Materials Act could encourage foreign investment into mining, exploration, and processing, building greater resilience across the supply chain. At the same time, material validation facilities and battery R&D centers would lower risks of adoption for new chemistries and make domestically produced materials more competitive. Strategic prioritization of resources, such as coal tar for synthetic anodes, can prevent diversion to non-battery industries and strengthen feedstock security, thereby enhancing India’s role in the global value chain.

The high capital intensity of the gigafactory and component manufacturing requires interventions that reduce upfront investment risks. Introducing a comprehensive capital subsidy framework, including support for land acquisition, plant and machinery, conversion charges, and exemptions on stamp duty and registration fees, would significantly lower entry barriers. Similarly, import duty exemptions on specialized equipment would reduce cost burdens during setup.
